paras: The lynching of Noah Griffin was the shooting of a Black man by forty masked men at Ocheeshee, Calhoun County, Florida, on Wednesday, August 15, 1888. Griffin had been accused of writing an insulting note to a young white woman, for which a group of white men had already whipped him and ordered him out of the county. The killing reached papers across the country through a single Apalachicola dispatch, and two papers, in Kansas and Minnesota, printed comments condemning it.

Ocheeshee lay in Calhoun County, and the dispatch reporting the killing was datelined Apalachicola, whose name the Washington Critic attached to the woman in the case. According to that dispatch, Griffin, described as "a negro," wrote an insulting note to a young white woman who shared his surname; her given name was printed as Kimmie, Kiminie or Simmie. None of the reports printed the contents of the note or any account from Griffin himself.

The woman showed the note to men whom the Richmond Dispatch called "some male friends" and other versions called "white men." Those men caught Griffin, gave him one hundred lashes, and ordered him to leave the county. When he did not go, forty masked men caught him and shot him to death. One version, printed in the Rock Island Daily Argus under an August 20 dateline, described the killers as "a gang of forty men" without mentioning masks and gave the whipping as 190 lashes.

The dispatch ended with the statement that no arrests had been made. No report of an inquest, arrest, indictment or trial appears in the coverage, and no account from a Florida newspaper was found. At the end of the year a roundup of the "Victims of Judge Lynch" listed Griffin under August 15 "in Callahoun County, Florida."

The story circulated almost entirely as one telegraphic dispatch, which appeared on August 19 in the Richmond Dispatch, the Savannah Morning News and the St. Paul Daily Globe. On August 20 it ran in the Washington Critic, the Rock Island Daily Argus and the Portland Daily Press, and on August 25 in the Macon Beacon of Mississippi. Headlines put the charge first: the Morning News used "Shot by Masked Men" over "A Negro Who Insulted a White Woman Suffers the Penalty," and the Globe used "Flogged and Then Shot" over "A Negro Lynched in Florida for Insulting a White Woman." These dailies presented the note as fact and added no comment on the killing.

Weekly news summaries in the Midwest and Dakota reduced the story to one line, pairing it with a lynching of two ranchers in Arizona and stating that Griffin "(colored)" was lynched "for insulting a white woman." A differently worded brief, in the Diamond Drill of Crystal Falls, Michigan, and later the Frontier of O'Neill, Nebraska, said he was shot "for writing insulting notes to a white girl."

Two papers protested. The Advocate of Leavenworth, Kansas, whose columns spoke for "our people" and for Black Republicans, reprinted the dispatch as "Lynched for Writing a Note" and asked, "How long will this hellish lynch-law reign? Will these devils ever see their shame?" The Western Appeal of St. Paul conceded that "Griffin did wrong to write the note" but insisted that "it certainly was not a crime worthy of death." Its editorial argued that white men insulted Black women far more often without punishment and concluded that the trouble arose "because the accused was Colored and the accuser white."

The Richmond Dispatch and the Savannah Morning News named the victim Nash Griffin, while the St. Paul Daily Globe, the Washington Critic and later reports named him Noah. The place name appeared in many spellings, among them Ocheeshee, Ocheehees, Ocheehee and Ochelhes. Some weekly briefs carried the phrases "on the 18th" or "on Saturday," but there the date belongs to the Arizona lynching in the same sentence; the dispatch and the year-end list both place Griffin's death on Wednesday, August 15.

reader.title: Lynching of Noah Griffin
bases: Forty masked men caught and shot Griffin to death after an earlier whipping and order to leave the county, with no arrests (A1, A2, A3).

Griffin was shot to death by forty masked men acting without any legal authority, as punishment for an alleged insulting note to a white woman and for not leaving the county as ordered (A1, A3); the dispatch itself calls it 'a lynching' and a year-end list counted him among the 'Victims of Judge Lynch' (A20).

Every account traces to one Apalachicola telegraphic dispatch (A1, A2, A3, A6) and its condensations (A8, A17); the year-end list (A20) adds a date but no independent detail, and no local Florida report was found.

accounts.gist: Griffin wrote an insulting note to a young white woman, was given 100 lashes by white men and ordered out of the county, and when he stayed forty masked men shot him to death; no arrests.

accounts.label: Year-end lynching list
accounts.gist: Counted Noah Griffin among the year's lynching victims, dated August 15, in Calhoun County, Florida.

framing.detail: Southern and national dailies ran the dispatch under 'A Negro Lynched', 'Shot by Masked Men' and 'Flogged and Then Shot', treating the note as fact and adding no comment.
Weekly news summaries reduced it to one line: Griffin '(colored)' lynched 'for insulting a white woman'.
The Advocate (Leavenworth), a paper speaking for Black Republicans, headed it 'Lynched for Writing a Note' and asked how long 'this hellish lynch-law' would reign.
The Western Appeal called it not 'a crime worthy of death' and blamed it on the accused being 'Colored and the accuser white'.

conflicts.note: Noah is the majority reading and the one in the year-end list (A20); Nash may be a telegraphic or typesetting variant.
All are spellings of the same Calhoun County place; Apalachicola is the dateline, attached by the Washington Critic to the woman (A5).
In the briefs the date phrase belongs to the Nagler lynching sharing the sentence; the year-end list puts the Naglers on the 17th and Griffin on the 15th, so Aug 15 is better supported.
190 appears in one version only and is likely a misprint.
